Wow.  Just wow.  This is quite possibly the greatest game I have played in a long time.  Orwell tells a brilliant narrative in an incredibly unique way, while also making an excellent point in regard to total surveillance (hence Orwell.)  What is essentially a point-and-click game manages to create incredible suspense, much better than the likes of many free-roam games.  Due to your choices affecting the outcome of the story, Orwell is worth more than one playthrough.  I have just finished my first, and I will be starting my second playthrough immediately.

Good game so far (I have completed Episode 3).  Gameplay is simple and easy to learn (select relevant information which pertains to an investigation).  The game presents a challenge when certain pieces of information conflict with one another or when not taking in the surrounding context can cause a deadly mistake.  This forces the player to be vigilant in their dealings with those they investigate.  The storyline draws the player in with a relevant topic, surveilance.  Though some read the game as making claims of whether or not mas surveilance is beneficial or harmful to society, I believe this is untrue.  The game simply asks the player to think about the subject by presenting a possible, though not necessarily probable, future scenario of mass surveilance in a fictional country.  Though obviously inspired by Orwell's work, the world presented by the game is very unlike Geourge Orwells "utopian" future.  The world is much more contemporary, which serves the game well by making the events and characters come to life more so than the bleak, hopeless world of 1984.  All in all, the simplicity of the game gets the player into the story quickly, while the relatable world and very familiar-feeling series of events and characters keep the player motivated to continue searching for the culprit of such heinous acts.  Those who are looking for a unique puzzle or logic experiene, or those who enjoy myustery novels, will most likely find thier money well spent on this title.

Long story:

This can be an exciting game if you're not one who likes nitpicking. However, if you do (which is maybe why you're drawn to it in the first place), you will pull some hairs out in rage and discontent.

The game focuses on monitoring an increasing set of data (news, websites, chat logs, phone calls etc) to look for leads in a specific case on which the game is built up. Whatever the game means is relevant will be highlighted, and you'll have the choice to either submit it to the investigators or ignore it. The info will also be rewritten, i.e. concentrated to what the game thinks it means.

This poses two problems - 1) the data YOU might think is highly relevant or more relevant isn't highlighted. And 2) the data you find may not be the data that will be submitted. For example, someone SUGGESTS to someone else that they do something. If you submit it, it's altered to say that the person PLANNED it. When talking about a crime that may or may not have occurred, this is a very important difference. Casually suggesting something and planning it is not the same. Everything you submit will be used by the police to decide which actions to take, so you might want to ignore that piece of info then.. if you can (explained further down).

Sometimes you find "contradicting info", and you can only pick one of the contradicting pieces (or ignore them altogether, of course). Sometimes these pieces of information don't contradict each other, but you still have to pick only one.

The game follows a story, and some key facts are needed in order to move it along. Once in a while you experience that the game doesn't progress, apparently because it won't continue until you've provided a key "fact" in the story. So you'll have to go through the stuff you ignored and guess which one the game wants you to submit before moving on. And yes, sometimes that includes incorrect information. Which causes rage quitting on my part, because the whole point of you making sure facts are provided is taken away.

The developers should have points for making a complex story and managing to implement this as a game - the way they have made it both simple, complex and engaging should be praised, as well as the psychological profiles of the suspects, showing how easily having inner access to their thoughts without having the proper context can lead to false conclusions. But the lack of preciseness and logical snafus in the interface makes what could have been an interesting take at the pros and cons of the surveillance society into a silly, semi-intellectual murder mystery for the masses.

A story-based game, played through a browser-like interface with the mouse. You play an investigator, picking through emails, web histories, phone calls and the like, investigating a group of potential terrorists. 

The storyline was engaging. The stylised interface was easy to use and the core mechanic of reading articles and picking the interesting points out of them was more fun than it sounds. The graphical style seemed fresh and exciting. I enjoyed the "1984" references.

The downsides are that the game is quite short, with low replayability due to its story-based nature. The story itself, while largely good, was missing a decent twist at the end. Unfortunately the characters were completely unlikeable, which meant I had little empathy with any of them.

The game itself seems designed to make you think about surveillance. It probably does, but the game itself is probably too opinionated to be objective.

Having said that, I enjoyed playing it and found it three hours well spent. It's worth the budget price, and the fact there's few similar games makes it worth playing.

Orwell is a fun, engaging, clever, brilliant, unique game that I would say is a mix of L.A. Noire, Her Story, Papers Please, and a touch of Telltale Games thrown in.

You go about solving a main crime which, along the way, you will discover a group of characters--all suspects. You do this by examining, accessing, reading through, and hacking into many different kinds of online resources (this would be the 'Her Story' aspect of it: A game where you get bits of the story unlocked, piece by piece and out of order, over time). As you go on, you will learn more and more about the suspects and characters and you need to try to figure out what information is relevant and what is not. What points of info is truth and what is false. What bits of knowledge and writings and conjectures are sarcasm or jokes and what is being said with true belief.... (the LA Noire side of it). Can you read between the lines and use logic and intuition to decide what will help you with the case and what may NOT be so smart to share with the database? 
You see, what you share with the database is totally up to you. This is the TellTale Game and Papers, Please side of it... in Papers, Please, you had the option, sometimes, to break the rules or turn your head to things based on what you believed to be morally right or true..or even just due to personal hunches or gut feelings.  What you choose to forever put into the database will affect the story, characters, and outcomes in a big way...there are multiple ways things could play out depending on if characters are free, in jail, or even killed. Sometimes you even have choices to make in the spur of the moment. Events that will happen in a few minutes (in game time) that you can either stop or allow to happen to see how things play out.


...but once you choose to document something into the database, the die is cast and you must live with your choices and  then all you can do is sit back and watch things play out and hopefully not live to regret how it all turned out.

Would strongly recommend.

[h1]Short, simple and yet so very much worth it.[/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] places the player in a role of an investigator for a mass surveillance system of the same name. After being assigned a case, the investigator's job is to gather information related to it using means provided by the system - relevant websites, private chats and so on. Information gathered is passed along to an 'adviser' who provides feedback and proceeds with other actions if necessary.

[u]The gameplay itself is rather simplistic.[/u] Shortly put, it consists of a lot of reading and putting highlighted information into the system (with a mere hold'n'drag method), though some of the data may conflict with each other and it will be up to the player to decide which information is correct. I do agree with those who say that [u]the mechanics could be improved[/u], as there is only a small amount of any form of detective work for the player to perform and some may feel like their hand is being held way too often. I should definitely mention though that [u]your choices do matter and influence the story.[/u]

Since I have mentioned it, it would be unforgivable not to say that [u]I found the story incredibly engaging[/u]. The [u]high-level of character development[/u] kept on working me over and over, changing how I feel about specific characters, making me alternate between love and hate for them, leading me on thinking I might have figured out the bad guy only to be presented an even more attractive suspect. 
One bad thing about it? [u]I completed the game in about four hours[/u], which is a liiittle bit short..

[u]The art style itself is very appealing, something which can also be said about the soundtrack[/u] (though do keep in mind it's meant to serve as background music - don't expect high energy or colourfulness!)

I don't think I would be too far off if I called [i]Orwell[/i] a novel which slowly unfolds itself before the player. In my opinion [u]it is a really great experience[/u] and [b]the developers released a demo version[/b] - make sure to play it to see if the game is for you! If you still have your doubts, which are very much understandable due to the simplistic gameplay, consider getting it on sale. It's worth it.

Ugh. So this is one of those games I wish Steam had a 'meh' review button for.

It started off strong. I really was hooked on my first playthrough. The concept is neat - you really feel like you're in charge of what information gets through and what doesn't. It took me about 3 hours (with reading everything) to get to the end my first time around. I was very disappointed it was so short - primarily because I honestly thought that there was going to be more than one case to investigate. Yeah - not the case.

Since I'm an achievement whore, I started another run through. This is where the game completely fails. It has, in my opinion, very little replay value. You start to learn that your choices don't actually do much to effect the outcome of the game. You can sort of control what happens to each person based on the information you submit, and occasionally certain things only unlock with certain choices....but other than that the dialogue is very very similar throughout. There is no fastforward button (that I could find) and no back button in case you screw up, which means you would have to completely start over if you mess up a chain of events to get a specific achievement.

It took two more playthroughs (three total) of two and a half hours each (aqain, can't skip ANY dialogue) to finish all achievements (gameplay time is a little higher because I would leave it running while doing other things). I was literally not at all invested in the game at this point because the changes in dialogue/direction are so small that they reduce replay value to nill.

I'm glad I got the game on sale because it's not worth $10, considering how short it is and how little replay value there is due to limitation of choice.

I dunno - the concept is unique and it was fun to play the first time around, so I do recommend it if you're looking for something intriguing to play on a rainy day. But I recommend getting it on sale.

An ultimately disappointing game. It's very short (~3 hours for a full run even if you are taking your time and reading everything), which I can forgive if the game is excellent but it's not.

The gameplay itself, as others have noted, is drag-and-drop pre-highlighted bits of text. Some of this text is mandatory for the game to proceed, some of it is optional. It's not always clear which, so it's easy to get stuck if you are doing a replay and want to see what happens if you ignore bits of evidence, and you may accidentially find yourself doing the same thing that you did last time.

A lot of the choices you make (up until episode 5) are relatively inconsequential, you'll get different text but the overall plot remains the same. Unfortunately there's no way to replay an episode to see what would happen if you did something else; supposedly this feature is being worked on, but in a choice-driven game this should have been a feature that shipped; Tell Tale has had this feature since The Walking Dead season 1.

I thought this game was going to be more about the surveillance state ala 1984, Person of Interest, etc. but I wouldn't say this is a good critique. True, you are reading other people's emails, but we're not investigating some political dissidents who said bad things about Great Leader, we're investigating an actual in-universe violent incident (and someone who potentially wants to commit more of these.) So while snooping through the emails of the suspects, it's not unreasonable to think that you are trying to catch people who legitimately committed a real crime. The game does try to railroad you a bit to force you to investigate someone who may not be the offender, which you can ignore, but this is pretty late in the game.

Some of the story beats just don't work; for instance, in the final parts of episode 4, [spoiler]information about your handler is leaked and the game forces you to drag-drop some of his personal information into his file. There's zero reason to actually do this, it's only to force the user to involve someone who clearly isn't a related to the crimes. And that would work if it was optional, but it's not. It's a "you are meant to feel bad right now" bit, and just falls flat.[/spoiler]

The "good ending" is pretty trash, [spoiler]everyone sings the freedom song and topples down statues and gives you a plaque for spilling the beans, ask Snowden how that's working out for him. It's rather corny.[/spoiler]

Overall had decent potential and the demo (episode 1) is pretty good, but fails in the end stretch.

Named after George Orwell, the author of the famous dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, comes a game about internet surveillance on potential 'terrorists'. You play the controller of a system called Orwell, sending information you feel is valid to your supervisor. This being a game about omnipresent government surveillance, you will see all manner of personal conversations, photos, bank statements etc. Is it all valid? Is all fair when the person you are investigating is the top suspect in a terrorist attack? What about if they are friends with the suspect? What about if they are a relative?

Much in the vein of Papers Please. this game will take your moral compass for a spin. I come from the UK, the soon-to-be Internet surveillance capital of the world. Orwell was a startling and interesting look into the world of surveillance. Can it be misused? Or can the use of it be justified? Yes and yes. This game did a miraculous job of showing you both sides of the argument with an interesting story to boot.

Think Papers, Please but with a strong story with multiple endings. You will make wrong decisions. You will make right decisions that feel like wrong decisions. Are the people of The Nation free? Are you really free?

Orwell has the bones of a great game but falls short in a few areas.  The game handholds you by highlighting the information you need throughout the game.  This would be fine if there were negative consequences for uploading irrelevant information.  But, you end up with a game comprised of clicking and dragging highlighted information to the correct profile.  This makes the game into more of a guided story.  One other complaint I have is how you cannot replay episodes on the same profile.  If you want to replay an episode, instead of giving you the option of loading a save file, you are forced to start a new game.  I guess this enforces the idea that your actions have impactful and lasting consquences, but it really comes off as more of an annoyance.

Having said all that, I did enjoy the game.  Fans of this genre or fans of "police state"-themed games will also find Orwell to be an enjoyable experience.  But, I cannot recommend the game to a broader audience unless either more content is added or a replay/save option is implemented.

EDIT: The developers have subsequently added a rewind feature.  Therefore, with my biggest complaint being rectified, I must change my recommendation from No to Yes.

Your mission is to "pilot" the test version of Orwell, a program that can monitor EVERYTHING on the internet - may it be mail, chat conversations, phone conversations, what files you've got on your computer, forums, medical records and ... yeah, a whole lot more. There has been a terrorist attack, a monument has been blown to smithereens and some people has been injured during the attack. The CCTV notices a woman prior known to the police and the first assignment is to find information about her, pinning her to the attack.

Gameplay wise, you're placed within a glorified web browser, more or less. To the left you have a profile and a map for all the known persons and their connections. To the right, you can read articles on the internet, chat conversations and all that good stuff. Then you drag the valuable information to the left panel and the story goes along.

If you like games such as Papers, Please, you may like this. There's a lot of story but it's also very dystopian. You could almost say it's a detective/mystery game, but then again, not. It's somewhat short, but it's one hell of a interesting ride, to put it that way. There's also some replayability, which makes it so I'll play it at least once more in the future, to get all the achivements and then see what'll happen when I choose to gather different information.

"The thoughts are free" ... or are they?

Orwell is a pretty neat little game about the potential dangers of openly accessible (or even not so openly accessible) data and the connections and conclusions you can draw from them.

You start out as an investigator for the project "Orwell", a surveillance system meant to protect the people and prevent crimes. 
After a bombing attack you are tasked, together with your supervisor, to find out who was behind the bombings and to prevent further ones.
As you dig deeper through websites and files, desktops and other material, you'll uncover more and more of the story, the motivations of the people responsible for the bombings and uncover some twists and turns throughout your investigations.

The gameplay is pretty simplistic. It's pretty much like surfing through a browser. You can access (predefined) websites and read through articles, blogs and also social media. Throughout the text you find some marked passages, which will help you with your investigation. You can connect these infos with a person and send these infos to Orwell. You can also decide to withhold some informations, letting events turn out differently in the process.

The story and events really sucked me in and were pretty thrilling. Slowly finding out more about the people, their connections to each other, and also be suprised by some twists, made the game very entertaining.

So if you don't mind simplistic gameplay and reading quite a lot and and the topic of data security doesn't turn you down, this is a little gem to keep an eye on.

I'd definitely recommend it.

The story is pretty good and there are multiple endings depending on player choice, but the gameplay is simple and repetitive, and probably not worth the price - would be a definite buy for 50% of the price.

Wow. This is like Papers Please for modern times. The moral dilemmas you're put in throughout this game are actually difficult! And they effect gameplay. There are only five "episodes", but within each episode, tons of choices. Do you, as an investigator using this Big Brother montoring system, report on someone's violent past and incriminate them when you believe they've turned it around and are a better person now? Does a character having a child mean their duty to their kid is more important than legality? And what about you -- the investigator -- and your role in all of this?

One playthrough took me about three hours, and this is a game that rewards multiple plays. Highly recommend!

Orwell is a difficult game to review.  You work as a member of a surveillance system and your task is to identify who is responsible for a bombing that happened on the city and why. For this task, you have a console to access internet pages, chats, phone calls and even computer files to establish profiles and identify information that could be exploited like email addresses and phone numbers.
There are no special graphics and the music is simple however in tune with the game´s purpose which is set up in five episodes, one for each day of work. The first episode is quite similar to a tutorial while the last one imposes several limitations on you and ethical choices.

I had a great time playing it (around 5 - 8 hours total) and I recommend it.

I don't normally write reviews, but felt I had to give a thumbs up to this one!

While it is undoubtedly largely linear, and it's more of an experience rather than a game, I was surprised how much - all logic aside - that I felt swept into the narrative and felt like I was having influence over things. There were a couple of times I even closed the game and went away to reflect. This game really is immersive.

To that end I'd recommend playing it in one or two sittings, and really investing into the experience. Put your earphones in and submerge yourself. Because by the end even though I know it's linear I feel like I've created the outcome. And I forget all the individual points I did, it just adds up in my mind that I had lots of control over the outcome.

What I also like is that for a game that could be heavy handed - and the name Orwell is hardly subtle - it was very nuanced. Not all the time, but the most part it had very good restraint. I also like that no one comes across as very good - it's all shades of grey and right up until the end it's muddy decisions and muddy outcomes. I don't feel I've won, I just feel I've made a decision and now I will live with it.

Grumbles are minor... your 'colleague' is often annoying, and spoon feeds you a bit too much. Information that is relevant in one context is dismissed out of hand another, which does at times snap you back to its linear nature. Chat sessions also keep moving when you're trying to read them at a different point in the thread - a small fix there would be welcome.

But great production values and style add to the polish to the game, and I highly recommend it.
